frames.title: Day 9 Agenda
frames.text:
Welcome to Day 9: Events, Meetings, CLE and Reputation.

We'll start with events and travel logistics, the biggest block today, then move on to meetings and video conferencing. After that comes compliance tracking and professional development, then stress and wellbeing, and we'll close with reputation and brand.

By the end of today, you'll be able to run events end to end, invites, intake forms and CLE included, keep meetings and compliance tracking on schedule, manage stress in a high-pressure role, and protect the organization's reputation.

frames.title: Events & Travel Logistics
frames.text: Section 1 of 5: Events and Travel Logistics. We'll run an event end to end, manage CLE for firm-hosted events, and handle high-stakes travel disruption.

frames.title: Running an Event End-to-End
frames.text:
A headcount tells you 58 people are coming. A list by name tells you that the client who matters most never finished registering. The whole event runs on that kind of detail.

First, track who has registered by name from day one. Next, plan who's attending what and what materials they need. Then, follow up with anyone whose registration is incomplete, while there's still time.

frames.title: Running an Event End-to-End
frames.text:
After that, compare the registration list with who actually came. Finally, write down what went wrong, so the next event is better.

Here's a situation to work through. Thorne & Partners is hosting a client appreciation evening for 60 guests in ten weeks. What's done by week eight, by week four and by the day before?

frames.title: Event Management Tips: Checklists, Run Sheets & the Day-Of Kit
frames.text:
Events look effortless when three simple documents are doing the work: a master checklist with an owner and date for every task, a run sheet that lays out the day minute by minute, and a contact sheet with every vendor and helper's phone number.

Most event problems are predictable, like a late caterer or a projector that won't connect. On the day, we're the calm center: we know where everything is and who to call.

frames.title: Event Management Tips: Checklists, Run Sheets & the Day-Of Kit
frames.text: First, we build the checklist from a template, working back from the date. Next, we write the run sheet: times, who leads each part, what it needs and what's next. Then we confirm every vendor 48 hours before.

frames.title: Event Management Tips: Checklists, Run Sheets & the Day-Of Kit
frames.text:
After that, we pack a day-of kit: printed sheets, spare badges, chargers, tape, first aid and the slides on a USB. Finally, we walk the venue before guests arrive, and debrief within a week.

Picture this. The client breakfast starts at 8:00. At 7:20 the caterer hasn't arrived, the projector won't connect to Elias's laptop, and two guests are early. Using your run sheet and contact sheet, what do you do in the next 10 minutes?

frames.title: Sending Invites: Calendar Invites & Event Invitations
frames.text:
A single wrong detail in an invite can make a whole meeting fail. A good invite answers five questions at a glance: what it is, when it is with the time zone, where or how to join, who's needed and what to prepare.

Event invitations follow a rhythm: a save-the-date, then the invitation with an RSVP date, reminders, and final details the day before.

frames.title: Sending Invites: Calendar Invites & Event Invitations
frames.text: First, we check availability, then send one invite, not a chain of emails. Next, a clear title, the right time zone, and the link, dial-in and location in the invite. Then a short agenda, anything to read, and who's required or optional.

frames.title: Sending Invites: Calendar Invites & Event Invitations
frames.text:
After that, for events: save-the-date six to eight weeks out, invitation three to four weeks out, reminders at a week and a day. Finally, we update the existing invite when things change, and cancel through the calendar.

Take a second with this one. Elias wants a call next week with a client in London, a partner in New York and an expert in Denver. How would you show the time so nobody gets it wrong, and what do you check before sending?

frames.title: Sending Intake Forms: Event Registration & New-Client Questionnaires
frames.text:
A good intake form means the event or the first meeting starts with everything you need, instead of a scramble. It asks only what's needed, in plain words, with the required fields clear, because every extra question means fewer people finish it.

And forms often collect personal or confidential information, so they're sent and stored securely. For new clients, the answers may also feed the conflict check.

frames.title: Sending Intake Forms: Event Registration & New-Client Questionnaires
frames.text: First, we use the firm's approved form tool, and the attorney approves client intake questions. Next, for events: name, organization, email, dietary and accessibility needs, sessions, and bar number and state for CLE. Then, for new clients: contact details, everyone involved, key dates and a short description, with documents through secure upload.

frames.title: Sending Intake Forms: Event Registration & New-Client Questionnaires
frames.text:
After that, we send it with a short note: why, the deadline and who to ask. We test the link first. Finally, we track completions, send one reminder and move the answers into the right system.

Here's one to try. Elias is meeting a potential new client, a small construction company, on Monday, and wants their details and everyone involved in their dispute beforehand. Pause the video and draft the six questions on your intake form, and the note you send with it.

frames.title: CLE Management for Firm-Hosted Events
frames.text:
When the firm hosts a CLE event, attendees are counting on us for credit they need to keep their licenses. The firm is the course provider, and it has duties to the state bars that approve the credit.

Every state has its own rules: whether the course needs approval in advance, how many minutes make an hour of credit, which categories like ethics apply, and what records we keep.

frames.title: CLE Management for Firm-Hosted Events
frames.text: First, months ahead, we find out which states attendees are licensed in and check each state's rules and deadlines. Next, we prepare the application: a timed agenda, speaker bios, materials and the hours and categories requested. Then we track attendance properly: sign-in and sign-out sheets, or the webinar's attendance report and any required codes.

frames.title: CLE Management for Firm-Hosted Events
frames.text:
After that, we issue certificates with the name, course, date, provider, hours, category and any approval number. Finally, we report to the states that require it and keep the file as long as each state says.

Here's a situation to work through. The firm is hosting a two-hour webinar in six weeks, with one hour of ethics, for attendees licensed in New York, New Jersey and California. What do you do this week, what do you collect at registration, and what happens afterwards?

frames.title: Speaker & Panelist Logistics for Conferences
frames.text:
When the executive is speaking at an event, the calendar entry is the smallest part of your job. Organizers have their own deadlines for bios, headshots, slides and technical needs. Miss one, and the speaking slot itself can be at risk. So you run it like a mini project.

First, make one checklist per speaking engagement, travel included, each item with its own due date. Next, confirm the format early: keynote, panel or fireside chat. Finally, before the event, send the executive one briefing: the time, the format, who else is speaking and what's expected.

Take a second with this one. Elias's slides are due Friday, and on Thursday he's still changing them. You also learn the venue projector only takes one type of cable. What do you send, and to whom?

frames.title: Sponsorship & Vendor Contract Basics for Events
frames.text:
A sponsorship is a real contract. When the firm sponsors an event, it's owed specific things: its logo in certain places, maybe a speaking slot or the attendee list. Noticing something's missing on the day is far better than noticing afterwards.

First, before the event, check each promised item against what's actually being provided. Next, keep the signed agreement with you during the event, in case there's a dispute. Finally, track what the sponsorship cost against the value it delivered.

Here's a situation to work through. The firm's logo is missing from the printed program, even though the agreement guarantees it. What do you do in the moment, and what do you follow up on afterwards?

frames.title: Live Event Moderation
frames.text:
Moderating a live event means watching actively for problems, not waiting for them to happen. Your job is to keep it running smoothly for the audience and the speaker, without distracting the speaker.

First, before it starts, confirm the executive's login and check their audio and video. Next, during the event, watch for sound drops, screen-share failures and questions to pass to the speaker. Then, for sessions that count toward professional credits, track attendance and times carefully. Finally, afterwards, confirm certificates and records, and document the session.

Think about this one. Halfway through Elias's webinar, 30 attendees drop off and chat fills with 'no sound.' Elias keeps talking, not aware. What do you do in the next 60 seconds?

frames.title: Post-Event Follow-Up & ROI Tracking
frames.text:
An event's real value comes from what happens after it. Meeting someone at an event is only a start. Without follow-up, that connection fades.

First, make notes during the event on who you met and what you talked about. Next, follow up within 48 to 72 hours, while they still remember the conversation. Finally, record who attended and what came of it in your normal relationship tracking system.

Here's a situation to work through. The firm spent $12,000 on three conferences this year. Elias asks, 'Were any of them worth it?' What would you need to have tracked to answer him?

frames.title: High-Stakes Travel Disruption Management
frames.text:
When travel falls apart, the real problem is rarely the flight itself. It's the deposition, the closing or the board meeting at the other end. So you triage: what has to happen, and in what order?

First, identify the fixed point: the one commitment he can't miss. Next, check the airline app while you're on the phone. Apps often show options faster than agents. Then, if no direct rebooking works, try another airport, another airline or a car for the final stretch, and warn the other side early if a delay is unavoidable.

frames.title: High-Stakes Travel Disruption Management
frames.text:
After that, send Elias one clear message: what happened, what you're doing and anything he needs to decide. Finally, once it's fixed, update everyone downstream: drivers, hotels and the meeting host.

Take a second with this one. Elias's connection to a closing-day meeting is cancelled, and the meeting can't move. Option one: a red-eye on another airline, landing two hours before. Option two: a private car for the last leg, costing much more but letting him sleep. How do you decide, and how do you present it?

frames.title: Meetings & Video Conferencing
frames.text: Section 2 of 5: Meetings and Video Conferencing. We'll cover everyday meeting notes, board meetings and minutes, and running video calls, from platform admin to troubleshooting.

frames.title: Everyday Meeting Notes & Action Items
frames.text:
A meeting is only as useful as what people do afterwards, and your notes decide that. Good notes capture three things: what was decided, what needs doing, and what's still open. And notes from meetings about legal matters may be privileged or confidential, so we label them and share them carefully.

First, before the meeting, we confirm the agenda and set up a template: attendees, decisions, actions and open questions. Next, we write decisions as clear statements. Then we write each action as a verb, an owner and a date. Without an owner and a date, it usually doesn't happen.

frames.title: Everyday Meeting Notes & Action Items
frames.text:
After that, we send the notes within 24 hours, with actions at the top. Finally, we add the actions to our tracker and check them before the next meeting.

Here's one to try. After a 45-minute Harlow strategy call, your notes say: 'Discussed deposition. Expert maybe. Budget concerns. Elias to think about it.' Pause the video and rewrite them so someone who missed the call knows exactly what happens next.

frames.title: Board Meeting Preparation & Minute Drafting
frames.text: Board minutes record what was decided and by whom, not who argued what. Most of a board meeting's work happens before anyone sits down: the agenda and the papers. And the minutes afterwards are a legal record, not a transcript. Both need precision, discretion and getting it right first time, because board mistakes are costly.

frames.title: Board Meeting Preparation & Minute Drafting
frames.text: First, confirm the agenda with the executive, and often the chair, well ahead, and send papers early enough to be read. Next, put the board pack together the same way every time. Then, during the meeting, capture who's present and absent, each motion, who seconded it and the exact result.

frames.title: Board Meeting Preparation & Minute Drafting
frames.text:
After that, write the minutes promptly, in neutral, factual language. Finally, send the draft round for corrections before it's finalized.

Here's a situation to work through. Your draft minutes say, 'Director Harlow strongly objected to the budget and was overruled after a heated debate.' How would you rewrite it, and why does it matter?

frames.title: Shareholder & Investor Meeting (AGM) Logistics
frames.text:
If an annual shareholder meeting doesn't have enough people present, none of its decisions count. An AGM has formal rules beyond a normal board meeting: legally required notice periods, a minimum number of attendees called a quorum, and often a bigger guest list.

First, confirm the required notice period for this meeting and jurisdiction well in advance. Next, track RSVPs against the quorum requirement. Finally, prepare the pack with the same care as a board meeting, plus any proxy and voting materials.

Take a second with this one. On the morning of the AGM, a shareholder turns up with a handwritten proxy for someone else, and the procedure doesn't say whether that's accepted. Who decides, and what should have been settled earlier?

frames.title: Executive Meeting Etiquette
frames.text: At executive level, small slips stand out: an open microphone, a late join or an unprepared executive. Etiquette here isn't stiffness; it's removing friction so the conversation gets full attention. And how you show up reflects on the executive.

frames.title: Executive Meeting Etiquette
frames.text:
First, give the executive a short note before the call: agenda, length, who's attending and their roles. Next, join a few minutes early and check the technology works, so problems get found before the executive arrives. Then, keep your own presence professional and low-key. Finally, handle the mechanics quietly, like muting noise, sharing documents and watching the chat.

Here's a situation to work through. Thirty seconds before Elias's call with a prospective client, you notice the invite used the wrong time zone and the client may have been waiting for an hour. What do you do right now?

frames.title: Video Conferencing: Platform Admin (Zoom/Teams/Meet)
frames.text:
Set up video calls properly beforehand, and most problems never happen. Running the platform means owning the settings, and Zoom, Teams and Meet each work a little differently, so know your firm's main one well.

First, before scheduling, confirm the key settings: waiting room, screen sharing, recording and registration. Next, use a pre-meeting checklist: test access, check logins and attach the agenda. Then, know how to manage people live: mute, remove, promote to co-host and switch screens. Finally, review the account's default settings regularly.

Take a second with this one. A client webinar for 200 people is set up like an internal meeting, and anyone can unmute and share their screen. Someone shares something inappropriate. What should the settings have been?

frames.title: Video Conferencing: Technical Troubleshooting
frames.text: When a call breaks, get it working first and work out why afterwards. Most video problems fall into a few predictable groups: login, audio and video, and screen sharing. A calm, step-by-step approach beats panic nearly every time.

frames.title: Video Conferencing: Technical Troubleshooting
frames.text:
First, for a login failure, check the link and the browser, then contact the platform's support. Next, for sound or picture problems, check the right device is selected, check permissions, then try leaving and rejoining. Then, before any important call, have a backup ready, like a phone number. Finally, record every problem, the fix and how long it took.

Here's a situation to work through. A client can hear everyone, but no one can hear the client. Walk through the checks in order, and what you say while you're fixing it.

frames.title: Compliance Tracking & Professional Development
frames.text: Section 3 of 5: Compliance Tracking and Professional Development. We'll cover CLE tracking, membership renewals, and ethics and gift compliance.

frames.title: Four SOPs That Keep Professional Development on Track
frames.text: Four simple procedures keep professional development on track, and each one prevents a specific failure. They cover event registration, attendance, team training and reputation.

frames.title: Four SOPs That Keep Professional Development on Track
frames.text: First, for registrations, check the provider is legitimate and approved before booking. Next, for attendance, save certificates in one audit-ready folder. Then, for team training, assess needs quarterly and track whether it worked.

frames.title: Four SOPs That Keep Professional Development on Track
frames.text:
After that, for reputation, keep bios current, watch for opportunities and escalate negative publicity immediately. Finally, don't skip the one that feels least urgent.

Here's a situation to work through. A negative article about the firm appears in a legal trade blog, and nobody notices for a week. Which procedure should have caught it, and what would it have told you to do?

frames.title: Quick Check
frames.text:
Quick check. Which SOP covers saving certificates in an audit-ready folder? Is it A, the Team Upskilling SOP, B, the Attendance Tracking SOP, C, the Event Registration SOP, or D, the Reputation and Recognition SOP?

Take a second.

The answer is B, Attendance Tracking. That's where completion evidence, like certificates and webinar reports, gets filed for audits.

frames.title: CLE / Compliance Tracking
frames.text:
Lawyers must complete continuing legal education, or CLE, every reporting period, and these deadlines don't get extended. A single total for the firm hides who's actually at risk. So you track each person: completed hours, remaining hours and their deadline.

First, flag anyone getting close while there's still time to act. Then, check the hours actually count: the right category and the right state.

frames.title: CLE / Compliance Tracking
frames.text:
After that, give reminders plenty of lead time. Finally, check the tracker against the certificates on file.

Here's a situation to work through. Elias has 18 of his 25 hours, still needs 2 ethics hours, and his deadline is in seven weeks. What do you flag today, and what do you check about the hours he already has?

frames.title: Planning Professional Development
frames.text:
Good training fits into people's real schedules, and it's judged by what people can actually do afterwards, not by how many people showed up. Attendance tells us the room was full; it doesn't tell us anyone learned anything.

First, offer online and in-person options where you can. Next, decide before the session how you'll judge whether it worked. Then, collect feedback right after the session.

frames.title: Planning Professional Development
frames.text:
After that, track results over time, so you can see which formats work. Finally, use what you learn to improve the next session.

Take a second with this one. Elias wants to know whether the new billing training worked. You have attendance numbers and a feedback survey. What's missing, and what can you still measure?

frames.title: Membership Renewals
frames.text:
Memberships, clubs and associations all renew at different times of year. Relying on the renewal notice, or on memory, is exactly how one quietly lapses, usually the one that mattered.

First, build a tracker with the name, expiry date, status and who follows up. Next, set reminders well before each expiry. Then, automate reminders once there are too many to remember.

frames.title: Membership Renewals
frames.text:
After that, check the terms and price haven't changed before renewing. Finally, review the list now and then for memberships nobody uses.

Here's a situation to work through. Elias's state bar membership, two practice-section memberships and a country club all renew within 60 days, and one card on file expires this month. Build the tracker rows, and decide what you'd do first.

frames.title: Ethics & Gift Compliance
frames.text:
Gift rules are stricter than most people's instincts. Something that feels like ordinary courtesy with a client, vendor or official can still break a rule, or look like an attempt to influence someone.

First, know the firm's gift policy before accepting or offering anything beyond small courtesies. Next, log any gift above the policy limit, even if it seems fine. Finally, take extra care with government officials and regulated parties.

Take a second with this one. A court-reporting firm offers you two concert tickets 'as thanks for all the business.' You'd love to go. What do you do?

frames.title: Professional Liability & Insurance Awareness
frames.text:
You don't need to understand malpractice insurance; you need to spot the warning signs and pass them on. Catching early signs of a possible claim gives the firm many more options than finding out late.

First, know where the insurance documents and renewal dates are kept. Next, if a client's language suggests serious unhappiness, like mentions of complaints or damages, flag it immediately. Finally, keep renewal and review dates on the compliance calendar.

Here's a situation to work through. A client's email says, 'We're considering our options given how this was handled.' What's your read, and what do you do beyond replying normally?

frames.title: Stress & Wellbeing
frames.text: Section 4 of 5: Stress and Wellbeing. We'll look at recognizing stress and burnout, techniques that work at a desk, and setting boundaries under executive pressure.

frames.title: Recognizing Stress & Burnout in High-Pressure Roles
frames.text:
A bit of pressure can actually help you focus. Burnout is different: it's what happens when stress keeps going for weeks with no relief, until you feel exhausted, detached and less effective. This job has its own pressures, like always being on call and carrying other people's deadlines.

It builds in stages, from healthy pressure, to strain, to chronic stress and finally to burnout, and the earlier stages are where it's easiest to turn around.

frames.title: Recognizing Stress & Burnout in High-Pressure Roles
frames.text: First, once a week, take two minutes to check in with yourself: energy, sleep, mistakes, and anything you keep dreading. Next, name the exact thing causing the stress, like late-night texts or unclear priorities. A specific problem has a specific fix.

frames.title: Recognizing Stress & Burnout in High-Pressure Roles
frames.text:
Then, watch the pattern for a couple of weeks before deciding what to change. Finally, if it lasts for weeks or affects your sleep, health or relationships, talk to your manager and consider support, like an employee assistance program or your doctor.

Take a second with this one. You've double-booked Elias twice this week, you're snapping at vendors and you check email at 11 every night 'just in case'. What's going on, and what are your first three steps?

frames.title: Stress Management Techniques That Work at a Desk
frames.text:
Think about when stress actually hits: mid-afternoon, three things due and the phone ringing. A weekend away doesn't help you in that moment. Something small you can do right where you're sitting does.

First, before a call you're nervous about, take a few slow breaths: count four in and six out. When you breathe out more slowly than you breathe in, your body gets the message to calm down. Next, when your head is spinning, get everything onto paper, then choose just one next step. One step is manageable; twenty isn't.

frames.title: Stress Management Techniques That Work at a Desk
frames.text:
Then, build small breaks into the day: stand up, stretch or walk for a few minutes every hour or so. Finally, end the day on purpose: look at tomorrow, write down your top three and close the inbox. That's how you actually switch off.

Here's a situation to work through. Elias calls in a rush: a court date moved, three meetings have to shift and a family event now overlaps. What do you do in the first five minutes to keep a clear head before you touch the calendar?

frames.title: Setting Boundaries & Managing Executive Pressure
frames.text:
When an executive is stressed, match their problem with calm facts and options, not with more stress. Boundaries are simply agreements: when you're available, how fast you'll reply and what counts as an emergency. Without them, everything feels urgent.

First, agree the basics in writing: your working hours, what's a real after-hours emergency and how to reach you for one. Next, when a new request crashes into existing work, ask, 'Which of these should move?' instead of silently taking on both.

frames.title: Setting Boundaries & Managing Executive Pressure
frames.text:
Finally, under pressure, use a simple pattern: 'I understand this is urgent. The filing is due at three. I can move the vendor call, or ask Maria to cover it.'

Take a second with this one. Your agreement with Elias says after-hours contact is for court deadlines and family emergencies. At 9:30 p.m. he texts: 'Can you check if the partner lunch is still on Friday?' What do you do tonight, and how do you raise it tomorrow?

frames.title: Recovery, Workload Conversations & Support Resources
frames.text:
Raising your workload early, with facts and options, is professional, not complaining. Rest isn't the opposite of good work; it's what makes good work possible. And help exists: many employers have confidential support programs, and in the US, anyone in crisis can call or text 988.

First, before the conversation, write down your regular tasks, the hours they take, what's slipping and two or three possible fixes. Next, when you take time off, hand over properly: access for your cover, an out-of-office message and a one-page status note.

frames.title: Recovery, Workload Conversations & Support Resources
frames.text:
Finally, find out where support is before you need it: your employer's program, your manager or HR, and the people you trust.

Here's one to try. For two months you've been working 55-hour weeks, and you're starting to make mistakes. You want to raise it with Elias without sharing personal health details. Pause the video and draft your first two sentences, and the options you'd bring.

frames.title: Reputation & Brand
frames.text: Section 5 of 5: Reputation and Brand. We'll cover protecting the brand online, awards and charitable coordination, and building an executive's media and speaking kit.

frames.title: Protecting the Brand Online
frames.text:
When someone posts a bad review, respond calmly and factually, and never argue in public. A negative review, handled well, can actually do more for the firm's reputation than ten positive ones, because everyone sees how you respond.

First, monitor mentions and reviews regularly; don't just wait for trouble. Then, apply 'need to know' to anything sensitive that comes up.

frames.title: Protecting the Brand Online
frames.text:
After that, draft a considered reply rather than reacting in the moment. Finally, escalate anything beyond a routine review, like legal threats or coordinated attacks.

Here's one to try. A former client posts a one-star review: 'Thorne & Partners never returned my calls and overcharged me.' Pause the video and draft the public reply, then decide what you'd check before posting it.

frames.title: Quick Check
frames.text:
Quick check. A client posts an inaccurate negative review. What's the best response? Is it A, argue publicly to prove the client wrong, B, delete or hide the review without responding, C, reply professionally and factually, without escalating the conflict, or D, ignore it and hope it disappears?

Take a second.

It's C. A calm, factual public response protects the brand better than silence or confrontation.

frames.title: Awards, Recognition & Charitable Coordination
frames.text:
Great nominations get missed simply because nobody tracked the deadline. Award applications have exact eligibility, exact materials and a firm deadline. Charitable commitments need the same care, because a promise isn't the same as a donation made and documented.

First, keep a simple tracker of awards worth pursuing: name, deadline, eligibility, materials and status. Next, confirm the criteria and materials well before the deadline. Then, for charitable pledges, track both the commitment and whether it was fulfilled.

frames.title: Awards, Recognition & Charitable Coordination
frames.text:
After that, keep records of donations, because they often matter for tax purposes. Finally, treat awards and charity as proactive reputation-building.

Here's a situation to work through. Elias pledged $5,000 to a legal aid gala and was nominated for a regional bar award due in three weeks. What goes in the tracker for each, and what documents do you keep?

frames.title: Building an Executive's Media & Speaking Kit
frames.text:
A ready media kit turns a last-minute press request into a same-day reply. It's a folder with the executive's current bio, a good headshot, key talking points and past coverage, and it's only useful if it's current.

First, keep a standing folder with a short and a long bio, a recent headshot and a one-page summary. Next, keep a running list of past media and speaking engagements. Finally, review and refresh the kit every quarter.

Take a second with this one. A journalist needs Elias's bio and headshot in two hours. The bio on file is over a year old and lists a role he no longer holds. What do you do, given the deadline?

frames.title: Practice Lab
frames.text: Now it's your turn. In today's Practice Lab, the Events, CLE and Reputation Tracker, you'll write the invitation and registration form for a firm CLE seminar, catch unconfirmed registrants, turn a strategy call into clean meeting notes, spot who's behind on CLE hours, answer a negative review and track which awards deadlines are still open.
